clue.text: Crate in dock transported by bird

indicators.note: whatever is transported by something is carried inside it, so one piece rides within the other

blocks.note: the jay is a noisy bird of the crow family
to dock a tail is to cut it short, to lop it

explanation.surface: A packing crate sitting on the quayside is carried off by a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crate' looks like a box but is slang for a battered old car; 'dock' looks like a harbour but is the verb meaning cut short.
explanation.definitionFit: Crate is informal slang for a rickety old motor car, which is exactly what a jalopy is.

clue.text: Tool that’s pieced together?

blocks.note: surface reading: a cutting implement from the workshop
setter's reading: the same word names a picture puzzle assembled from interlocking pieces

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is both a narrow-bladed saw for curved cuts and the puzzle whose pieces were originally cut with one; the question mark flags the double reading.
explanation.definitionFit: A jigsaw is a power saw for cutting curves, and also the name of a picture puzzle that people fit together piece by piece.

clue.text: Unsophisticated type with hundred to invest in shockingly sour wine

indicators.note: something done shockingly is done in a disordered, upsetting way, so these letters are thrown into a new order
money invested in something is put inside it, so one piece goes into the other

blocks.note: a lamb is an innocent, naive person
taken as written, to be rearranged
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: A naive drinker with a hundred to spend buys some dreadfully sour wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sour wine' reads as a phrase, but 'sour' is the letters to be rearranged and 'wine' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Lambrusco is a sparkling red Italian variety from the Emilia region, so it is one example of the drink named.

clue.text: Little hairy feature bothered the masculine cop

indicators.note: someone bothered is flustered and disturbed, so these letters are disturbed into another order

blocks.note: fifteen letters taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A macho police officer is irritated by some small hairy thing.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole fifteen-letter phrase after 'bothered' is rearranged; spotting that the letter count matches the enumeration is the way in.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin, narrow line of hair along the upper lip is a small facial growth, so a modest hirsute adornment.

clue.text: Get up and out back

blocks.note: to get up from a seat is to stand
a light that is out is off

explanation.surface: An instruction to rise and leave by the rear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' looks like a direction to go, but it is the definition: in rugby, the backs are the players behind the scrum, and the stand-off (fly-half) is one of them.
explanation.definitionFit: In rugby union the stand-off half plays behind the forwards, making that player one of the team's backs.

clue.text: A shade late when disorganised

indicators.note: disorganised things are out of their proper order, so these letters need rearranging

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is running slightly late because they are disorganised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A shade late' reads as 'a little late', but 'A shade' is the definition, a colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Teal is a dark greenish-blue colour, so it is one particular hue or tint.

clue.text: Romantic movie opening in part of London

blocks.note: Notting Hill is the 1999 romantic comedy starring Hugh Grant and Julia Roberts
a gate is an opening in a fence or wall

explanation.surface: A romance film has its premiere somewhere in London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening' looks like a film premiere, but it is a noun for a gap you walk through.
explanation.definitionFit: Notting Hill Gate is a district and Underground station in west London, at the top of the Notting Hill area.

clue.text: Old relative defending a group

indicators.note: to defend something is to stand around it as protection, so one piece surrounds the other

blocks.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old
sis is short for sister
taken as written

explanation.surface: An elderly family member protects a gathering of people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Group' suggests any collection of people, but here it means a pop group: Oasis was the Manchester band of the Gallagher brothers.
explanation.definitionFit: Oasis was a hugely successful British rock band of the 1990s, so a musical group by example.

clue.text: A little puffin, is he drooled over?

indicators.note: a little of something is only a portion of it, so the letters are a part taken from the words that follow

blocks.note: the run of letters spans the end of the bird, two whole words and the start of the last

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a cute baby seabird is being cooed and slobbered over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' looks like part of the phrase 'drooled over', but it stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: When something is over it has ended or been completed, which is what done or completed means.

clue.text: Time in silence, playing on computer?

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it, so the first piece is placed within the second

blocks.note: min is the abbreviation for minute, a unit of time
to gag someone is to silence them

explanation.surface: Hours spent quietly absorbed in a computer game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silence' looks like a noun for quiet, but it is the verb meaning to stop someone speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: Playing video games on a computer or console is commonly called gaming; the question mark notes it is not the only kind of play.

clue.text: Role exists with an adherent to the cause

blocks.note: an actor's role is a part
to exist is to be, so 'is'
taken as written

explanation.surface: A job description involving a committed supporter of some movement.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue simply strings three short pieces together; 'with' just joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A partisan is a committed supporter of a party or movement, someone devoted to its aims.

clue.text: Northbound English ship shortly heading for Latvia, leaves

indicators.note: in a down entry, travelling north means reading upwards, so the letters run backwards
made short means cut off at the end, so the final letter is dropped
the heading of a word is its front, so only its opening letter is kept

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
a cutter is a small sailing ship, here missing its last letter
the first letter of the country

explanation.surface: An English vessel sailing north, soon bound for Latvia, departs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' looks like the verb 'departs' to finish the voyage, but it is the plural noun for foliage, and a salad plant is all leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: Lettuce is the leafy salad vegetable eaten for its foliage, so it is literally a head of edible greens.

clue.text: Points made by travellers in Israel after diversion around motorway

indicators.note: a diversion sends traffic off its usual route, so the letters are taken off their usual order
around means encircling, so the rearranged letters wrap about the other piece

blocks.note: a loose shortening; the printed clue appears to have meant 'Israeli', which supplies the same extra letter
the country's name taken as written, to be rearranged
M is the prefix of British motorway names, as in the M1

explanation.surface: Tourists in Israel score points after being sent on a detour round a highway.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged letters need two Is, one more than Israel has; the clue most likely intended 'Israeli', and the motorway sits in the middle of the result.
explanation.definitionFit: Air miles are loyalty points earned by flying passengers, redeemable for further flights or rewards.

clue.text: Long to see American partner

blocks.note: to long for someone absent is to miss them
US is short for the United States, hence American

explanation.surface: Someone is eager to visit their partner in America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long to see' reads as one yearning phrase, but only 'Long' is wordplay; 'to see' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Missus is informal, chiefly British slang for a man's wife, that is, his spouse or companion.

clue.text: Extraordinary detail under roof of Chinese fortress

indicators.note: something extraordinary is out of the ordinary, so the letters leave their ordinary order
the roof is the top of a structure, and the top of a down word is its first letter
in a down entry, one piece under another comes after it in the reading order

blocks.note: the first letter of the word
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Remarkable ornamentation beneath the eaves of a Chinese stronghold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extraordinary detail' reads as a description, but the adjective tells you to rearrange the noun's letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A citadel is a stronghold built to protect a city, so it is a fortified castle or keep.

clue.text: Wonderful, not that then?

blocks.note: first meaning: informal praise for something extraordinary
second meaning: if not that, then a different thing altogether

explanation.surface: Someone rejects an option as merely wonderful, wanting another.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma separates two readings of one phrase: slang approval, and the literal 'a different thing'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is slang for remarkable or outstanding, and literally names an alternative thing instead of the one rejected.

clue.text: Imaginary line, moulds glued on it

indicators.note: to mould something is to reshape it, so these letters are reshaped into a new word

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A craftsman shapes something and sticks a fine line on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moulds' could be the fungus, but it is the verb meaning shapes.
explanation.definitionFit: A line of longitude is a meridian, an invisible north-south arc drawn on maps but not existing physically on Earth.

clue.text: Entire distribution of power in cult, strange

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it, so the first piece is placed within the second

blocks.note: P is the symbol for power in physics
a sect is a cult or religious faction
rum is old British slang for odd or peculiar

explanation.surface: The way power is shared out inside a cult is entirely odd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' is not an anagram signal here; it supplies a word meaning odd, which comes last.
explanation.definitionFit: A spectrum is the full range of something, from one extreme to the other, covering every value in between.

clue.text: The way said to incur pain, on being given treatment

indicators.note: treated material is processed and worked over, so these letters are worked into a new order

blocks.note: thirteen letters taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is told that a medical procedure is bound to hurt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Said' looks like the start of reported speech, but 'The way said' is the definition: the way a word is spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: Pronunciation is the manner in which a word is spoken, so it describes how something is uttered.

clue.text: Seed that’s very little, cut

indicators.note: cutting something trims it, so the end letter is chopped off

blocks.note: informal plural for a trivial sum of money, as in a paltry wage

explanation.surface: A tiny seed is being cut.
explanation.walkthrough: The informal plural for a trivial sum loses its final S.
explanation.definitionFit: The edible kernel inside a groundnut pod is botanically a legume seed, so it is a fair example of one.

clue.text: Old units, pieces of copper?

blocks.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
pieces are bits

explanation.surface: Historic measures, perhaps lumps of copper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' might be a policeman in British slang, but here it is the metal, by its chemical symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: The cubit was an ancient measure of length, roughly the distance from elbow to fingertip.

clue.text: Big on elastic — by the sound of it?

definitions.text: Big on elastic — by the sound of it?

indicators.note: elastic stretches and changes shape, so these letters are stretched into another arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is a great fan of elastic, or so it sounds.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue describes the noise of something bouncing on elastic, while two words of it supply the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is the comic noise made by something springy recoiling, like a bungee or rubber band.

clue.text: Beelzebub’s punishment, expect him to shoot?

blocks.note: first meaning: the flames of damnation the devil inflicts
second meaning, read as two words: an expletive followed by the order to open fire, as Beelzebub might command

explanation.surface: The devil's torment, and a warning that he is about to fire.
explanation.walkthrough: Split into two words, the answer becomes an oath plus a command to shoot, the kind of order the devil just named might bark.
explanation.definitionFit: Hellfire is the eternal burning said to torment sinners in hell, the domain ruled over by Satan.

clue.text: Gathered by seamstress, a ripped Indian dress

indicators.note: something gathered by a group is held among them, so the letters lie within the neighbouring words

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word, through the article, into the start of the last

explanation.surface: A dressmaker gathers the fabric of a torn traditional garment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gathered' sounds like sewing pleats, a neat fit with the seamstress, but it signals that the letters sit inside the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A sari is the long draped cloth garment traditionally worn by women in India and South Asia.

clue.text: Garment in a fashionable company stolen by cad

indicators.note: something stolen is carried off inside the thief's possession, so one piece is held within another

blocks.note: taken as written
what is in is fashionable
Co is the abbreviation for company
a rat is a scoundrel or cad

explanation.surface: A designer garment belonging to a stylish firm is pinched by a rogue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cad' is an old British word for a dishonourable man, so a rat.
explanation.definitionFit: A raincoat is a waterproof outer coat, one particular item of clothing.

clue.text: Planet: go beyond it

indicators.note: beyond means further along, so this piece follows the other in the reading order

blocks.note: 'it' is old slang for sex appeal, abbreviated SA
a go in a game is a turn

explanation.surface: An instruction to travel past a planet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go' looks like a verb of motion but is the noun for a player's turn; 'it' for sex appeal is a long-standing crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun, the ringed gas giant of our solar system.

clue.text: Drawing man, I get out first of crayons

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or disordered, so these letters are put into a different order
the first of a word is its opening letter, so just that one is kept

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: An artist sketching complains he is getting out his crayons first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawing' suggests sketching, which crayons reinforce, but it means attracting, as a magnet draws metal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something drawing pulls things towards it, and a magnet attracts iron, so the adjective means attracting.

clue.text: Sorrowful whistler secured by stake

indicators.note: something secured by another is held fast inside its grip, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: a referee blows a whistle to control a match
a stake is a wager, a bet

explanation.surface: A mournful bird or person is tethered to a post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stake' looks like a wooden post to tie something to, but it is the money put on a wager; 'whistler' is the match official.
explanation.definitionFit: Bereft describes someone deprived of a loved one and so grieving and desolate.
